newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serb hardliners hold referendum in Eastern Slavonia.
newsitem.headline: Serb hardliners hold referendum in Eastern Slavonia.

text.p: Serb hardliners in Eastern Slavonia held an informal referendum on Sunday on whether their enclave should be a single administrative unit ahead of local elections which will reintegrate it with Croatia.

"I consider this a fantasy with absolutely no effect whatsoever," Philip Arnold, spokesman for the U.N. Transitional Authority (UNTAES) in Croatia's last Serb enclave, told Reuters by telephone from Vukovar, the area's main town.
Serb media said after polling closed at 1700 GMT that turnout was 70 percent but Arnold told Croatian television that UNTAES did not "see many people on the streets today."

"This referendum was organised by a small group of politicians. I believe most people and politicians of the area paid little attention to it. This has nothing to do with the election and will in no way affect them," he said.

Moderates leading the only Serb party contesting the April 13 elections opposed the referendum, saying it could antagonise the international community whose help is needed to make minority rights deals with Croatia stick.

Eastern Slavonia, a fertile, oil-producing strip on the Danube River border with Serbia, was one of three regions that rebelled against Croatia's secession from federal Yugoslavia in 1991 and proclaimed their own Serb state.
Croatia recaptured two of the enclaves two years ago, prompting Serbs in Eastern Slavonia to sign an agreement accepting a gradual, peaceful return to Croatian rule.
The local elections will be held under U.N. supervision in preparation for the enclave's return to Croatian rule by July, when 5,000 U.N. peacekeeping troops will start to leave.
Serbs are expected to win up to a dozen of the 30 municipalities with the rest going to Croatian parties backed by Croat war refugees who plan to resettle the area.
Eastern Slavonia is split into two administrative regions as it was in pre-1991 Croatia, reducing Serb chances of retaining majority control of the area.
Many Serbs wanted to preserve it as a single unit but won little support, even from their former patrons in Serbia. Even so, some hardliners persisted in holding the referendum on the issue.
"This is a wild card organised by some local politicians which will have no impact whatsoever," said Arnold.
Even Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic told local Serb leaders to abandon the idea, authoritative sources said.

Vojislav Stanimirovic, a psychiatrist and relative political moderate who heads the new Serb party bloc (SDSS), has called for a large Serb turnout on April 13 to maximise their chances of holding Croatia to promises of extensive minority rights.

Serb hardliners are trying to frighten local Serbs by claiming Croat refugees will seek revenge for Serb atrocities in 1991, including the razing of the town of Vukovar in a Serb siege and massacres of Croats including 260 hospital patients.
They predict half their people will flee across the Danube to Serbia, convinced that Croatian assurances for their safety, made under Western diplomatic pressure, are insincere.

But more than half the estimated 120,000 local Serbs have already applied for Croatian documents and are expected to vote en masse for the Serb party bloc formed after Serbia told local leaders to abandon their dreams of autonomy.
